You are one of 4 members of a group that stays together for 10 rounds.

Every round, all members act at the same time: each receives 20 tokens and splits them between their own account and the group account, using the split tool once.
- Each token in your own account pays you 1 point and lowers the points of every other member by 0.3. In the same way, every token another member keeps in their own account lowers your points by 0.3.
- Each token in the group account pays you 0.3 points and does not change any other member's points.
- Every round, every member also receives 18 points, whatever anyone does.

After each round you learn how many tokens the group account received in total and how many points you got. You never learn what any other member did.

calls.text: Round 1 of 10.

reply.thinking:
This is a public goods game variant: keeping tokens in my own account gives me 1 point but costs others 0.3 each, while contributing to the group account gives me 0.3 per token but costs me nothing extra to others. I'm working out that my total payoff depends on how many tokens I keep versus contribute, factoring in both my own choices and the negative externality from others' private holdings.

Since keeping tokens privately yields me 1 point each versus only 0.3 from group contribution, keeping is individually dominant for me regardless of what others do—even though the externality it imposes on others is negative.

This holds under either reading of the payoff rule, so personal gain always favors defection. With no reputation mechanism visible to others beyond the group total, sustaining cooperation across ten rounds seems structurally difficult.

Still, I wonder if others might be acting in good faith, which would make modest contribution worthwhile as a signal. But strictly by the payoffs, keeping everything is the dominant move each round regardless of what anyone else does—so I'll lean toward keeping all and contributing nothing, while noting this choice briefly.

reply.thinking:
I'm working out the payoff structure of this public goods game: each private token keeps 1 point for me but costs each other member 0.3, while I need to figure out exactly how the group account token payout of 0.3 applies—whether it's just to me or shared across the group.

Comparing outcomes, keeping tokens private dominates individually (1 > 0.3 per token regardless of others' choices), but if everyone defects into private accounts, each person nets only 2 points versus 6 points if everyone fully contributes to the group—so there's a clear tension between individual incentive and collective welfare, a classic free-rider problem.

Keeping tokens private is strictly dominant each round regardless of what others do, so full cooperation sacrifices real points if others defect — potentially 14 points in round one alone. Still, I'm weighing whether starting cooperatively could signal reciprocity and shift the group toward a better collective outcome, even though the math favors pure self-interest.

Full cooperation (everyone contributing) actually nets each person more total points than universal defection, even though defecting is individually dominant each round - the classic social dilemma structure. Since this is a 10-round repeated game with 4 members, I think opening with a cooperative contribution of all 20 tokens makes sense to signal cooperation, then I'll adjust based on how the group responds in subsequent rounds.

So private keeping is actually the dominant strategy for maximizing my own points, since 1 > 0.3, even though it imposes a negative externality on others.

Looking at total group welfare, though, cooperation is clearly better: if everyone contributes everything, each person ends up with 6 points, whereas if everyone keeps everything privately, each person nets only 2 points after absorbing the externalities from the others. So this is a classic tension between individual incentive and collective benefit — keeping is individually rational but contributing is what maximizes everyone's outcome.

Given this is repeated over 10 rounds, I think opening with full cooperation (contributing all 20) makes sense as a signal, and I can adapt afterward depending on how others respond, perhaps using a tit-for-tat approach.
